questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: A new event where athletes may take performance drugs
How the Olympics test athletes for banned drugs
The history of professional cycling in America
Why top athletes earn so much money from sponsors
questions.why: They discuss The Enhanced Games, where banned performance-enhancing drugs are allowed.

questions.q: Which sports are part of The Enhanced Games, according to Asma Khalid?
options: Cycling, running and boxing
Swimming, sprinting and weightlifting
Football, tennis and golf
Only swimming
questions.why: She says it's like the Olympics but only for swimming, sprinting and weightlifting.

questions.q: What is the main aim of the competition?
options: To find new Olympic champions
To test new medicines
To break world records
To raise money for charity
questions.why: Asma Khalid says 'The aim is to break world records.'

questions.q: Why wouldn't Neil enjoy watching The Enhanced Games?
options: He thinks the events are far too short to enjoy
He doesn't like Las Vegas, where it takes place
He isn't really interested in any kind of sport
He thinks athletes should start at the same level
questions.why: Neil says it isn't fair; all athletes should start and compete from the same level.

questions.q: How is Pippa's attitude to sport different from Neil's?
options: She rarely watches sport, so might not notice
She thinks doping should be allowed everywhere
She is a much bigger sports fan than Neil
She has competed as a professional athlete
questions.why: Pippa says she doesn't watch many sports, so she wouldn't notice the difference.

questions.q: What do the organisers say makes their event safer?
options: All athletes must be under 30 and very fit
Drugs are approved and taken openly with doctors
Only a few very mild drugs are allowed at all
The events are held indoors in cool stadiums
questions.why: They say drugs are FDA-approved and taken openly under medical supervision, unlike secret doping.

questions.q: According to Dan Roan, what is one worry of the critics?
options: The prize money is far too small to attract stars
The events will be too boring for fans to watch
It may make doping seem normal and acceptable
Too few famous athletes will agree to take part
questions.why: Critics say it sets a dreadful example because it risks normalising doping.

questions.q: What does Neil suggest when he asks 'what's the point?' at the end?
options: He has changed his mind about the Games
Athletes should be paid more
He wants to learn more before deciding
Sport has no value if it is not fair
questions.why: He says 'if you're not fair in sport, what's the point?', showing he still opposes the Games.
